title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about conducting research well: running a project with rigour and holding it to ethical and academic integrity. By the end you will be able to justify the principles that govern ethical research, handle participant data responsibly, and sustain integrity and rigour across a project from proposal to dissertation.

This is not study in the abstract. As an advanced student you are undertaking, or about to undertake, your own substantial research, where these are decisions you must make and defend rather than rules to recall. Getting them right protects the people your research touches and the standing of the work itself.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: justify the ethical principles that must govern a research project and how approval is secured
handle research data responsibly, securing confidentiality, informed consent and anonymity
sustain research integrity and rigour across a project, from proposal to dissertation.

title: In real academic practice
body: Running research with integrity is what separates work that can be trusted from work that merely looks finished. Every ethics application you complete, every participant whose data you protect, and every decision you can defend to an examiner draws on the same habits. Build them now and they carry into any research you go on to do, in study or in professional life.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, research ethics and integrity: the principles that govern sound research and how approval is secured. Second, handling research data responsibly: the duties you owe the people who provide your data. Third, rigour across the research project: sustaining integrity from proposal to dissertation. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, projects and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, study or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can justify the ethical principles that must govern a research project and how approval is secured.
I can handle research data responsibly, securing confidentiality, informed consent and anonymity.
I can sustain research integrity and rigour across a project, from proposal to dissertation.

title: Orientation
body: When you run your own research, ethics stops being an abstract value and becomes a set of decisions you have to make and defend. Most students first meet this as the research-ethics form, completed after an ethics module and before any data is collected. Behind that form sit the principles this lesson is about.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are working at the level of a researcher, not a reader of research. The aim is not to recognise that ethics matters, which you already know, but to judge a design against established principles and to see where it is sound and where it is exposed.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: justify why ethical conduct is an expression of academic integrity rather than a bureaucratic hurdle
evaluate a research design against the six ESRC principles of ethical research
anticipate the ethical issues a research-ethics application in {{context}} would need to address.

title: Concept: definition
body: Research ethics is the set of principles that govern how research is conducted so that it benefits people without doing them harm. The research-ethics form is only the mechanism through which an institution checks this; the principles are the real substance. Completing the form well means acknowledging the issues those principles raise, which is why ethical conduct is part of academic integrity rather than a separate hoop. A study that treats approval as a box to tick can still be ethically weak, while a study designed around the principles is sound whether or not anyone inspects it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a piece of research you are planning or have read closely. Which of the six principles would be hardest to satisfy, and why? What would you change in the design to meet it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Research ethics is the substance behind the ethics form, not the form itself. You can now justify ethical conduct as an expression of academic integrity, evaluate a research design against the six ESRC principles, and anticipate the issues an ethics application must address. The next lesson turns to the duties you take on once you start collecting data.

title: Orientation
body: The moment you collect data, you take on responsibilities to the people who gave it to you. These are not only courtesies; some are legal obligations. This lesson is about what you owe participants and how you meet those duties in practice.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are handling real data from real people, not reading about the idea of it. The aim is to apply the duties confidently to your own decisions about storing, sharing and reporting data, and to know when a situation calls for expert advice.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: apply the researcher's duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity to the handling of data
justify the additional care required when participants are children or otherwise vulnerable
appraise how participant data in {{context}} should be secured, shared and anonymised.

title: Concept: definition
body: Handling data responsibly rests on three duties. Confidentiality is a legal obligation to keep data that is not in the public domain secure. Consent means securing participants' agreement, usually in writing, before their data is shared. Anonymity means reporting responses so that individuals cannot be identified, for example as Participant A or Participant B. Where participants are children or otherwise vulnerable, these duties tighten, and your tutor or the research ethics committee can advise on the further safeguards needed.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the data your research would collect. Who could be harmed if it were not kept confidential, and what is the single most important step you would take to protect participants?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Orientation
body: Rigour and integrity are easy to promise at the start of a project and hard to sustain to the end. The dissertation is where they are finally tested, because it draws every part of your research together on a grander scale. This lesson is about keeping the thread intact from proposal to submission.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: As an advanced student you are expected to own the quality of your own research. The aim is to see rigour as something sustained across stages, and to be able to defend your decisions rather than simply describe what you did.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: articulate how integrity, transparency and accountability are sustained across a research project
evaluate whether a project upholds rigour from its proposal through to the dissertation
defend the decisions you would make to keep a project in {{context}} rigorous and accountable.

title: Concept: definition
body: Integrity, transparency and accountability are principles you sustain, not steps you complete. Across a project they show up as decisions that line up: the questions in your proposal, the method your ethics approval covers, and the findings your dissertation reports should tell one coherent story, with any departure explained. The dissertation represents the ultimate test of your competencies, because it is where a careful reader can see whether that rigour held throughout or was assembled at the end.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at a research project you are undertaking or planning. Where is the greatest risk that your proposal, your approved method and your final write-up will drift apart, and how would you keep them aligned?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Rigour is not a stage but a thread that runs from proposal to dissertation. You can now articulate how integrity, transparency and accountability are sustained, evaluate whether a project holds together across its stages, and defend the decisions that keep research rigorous. The dissertation is where that sustained integrity is finally tested.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Conducting research well is now something you can describe and defend. You can justify the ethical principles that govern a project and explain how approval is secured, treating the ethics form as the substance of integrity rather than a hurdle. You can handle participant data responsibly, protecting confidentiality, securing consent and preserving anonymity. And you can sustain integrity and rigour across a whole project, so that proposal, method and dissertation tell one coherent story. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, rigour and ethics are things you practise in every piece of research you undertake. Each ethics application, each dataset you protect, each decision you can account for, is this habit at work. It is also what research and professional practice reward most: work whose integrity can be shown, not just asserted, travels well beyond your degree.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The six principles of ethical research
body: The ESRC sets out six principles that together maintain research integrity. Open each to see what it asks of your research.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all six.

_items.title: Benefit and harm
_items.body: Research should aim to maximise benefit for individuals and society while minimising risk and harm. Before you begin, you weigh what the work could contribute against the burden or risk it places on those who take part.

_items.title: Rights and dignity
_items.body: The rights and dignity of individuals and groups must be respected throughout. This shapes how you recruit participants, how you ask your questions, and how you report what they tell you.

_items.title: Voluntary, informed participation
_items.body: Wherever possible, participation should be voluntary and appropriately informed. People decide to take part knowing what the research involves, and they are free to decline or withdraw without penalty.

_items.title: Integrity and transparency
_items.body: Research should be conducted with integrity and transparency. You are open about your methods, honest about your findings, and clear about what the evidence will and will not bear.

_items.title: Responsibility and accountability
_items.body: Lines of responsibility and accountability should be clearly defined. Everyone involved knows who is answerable for each part of the work, from data storage to supervision.

_items.title: Independence and conflicts of interest
_items.body: The independence of research should be maintained. Where a conflict of interest cannot be avoided, you declare it openly rather than letting it quietly shape the work.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two researchers preparing the same small interview study for ethical approval.

{{learner-a}} treats the ethics application as a form to clear. The consent wording is vague about how recordings will be stored, participation is described as expected rather than voluntary, and a conflict of interest with the host organisation goes unmentioned. The design may still gain approval, but it sits uneasily against the principles of informed participation, transparency and declared interest.

{{learner-b}} reads the same design against each principle in turn. Participation is made genuinely voluntary and informed, storage and responsibility are spelled out, and the conflict of interest is declared openly. Nothing about the study is hidden, so the application documents a design that is sound rather than merely permitted.

Both researchers will submit a form. Only {{learner-b}} used the principles to improve the research itself, which is what treating ethics as integrity rather than paperwork means.

title: Before you submit an ethics application
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to test a research design against the principles before you submit it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I shown how the research maximises benefit and minimises risk and harm?
Have I respected the rights and dignity of everyone the research touches?
Is participation genuinely voluntary, with participants properly informed?
Have I been transparent about my methods and honest about their limits?
Are the lines of responsibility and accountability clearly defined?
Have I declared any conflict of interest that I cannot avoid?

title: Formative check: ethics and integrity
displayTitle: Why is ethical conduct best understood as an expression of academic integrity rather than a bureaucratic hurdle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is ethical conduct an expression of academic integrity?

_items.text: Because the principles that shape ethical research are the same values of honesty and responsibility that underpin academic integrity.
_items.feedback: Yes. Ethics and integrity rest on the same values.

_items.text: Because the ethics form is required before a university will award a degree.
_items.feedback: That makes it a hurdle; it does not explain why ethics is integrity.

_items.text: Because ethical approval guarantees that the research findings will be correct.
_items.feedback: Approval concerns conduct, not whether findings are correct.

_items.text: Because completing the form quickly leaves more time for data collection.
_items.feedback: Speed has nothing to do with why ethics is integrity.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Ethical conduct and academic integrity rest on the same values of honesty and responsibility.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about shared values, not procedure.
_incorrect.final: Ethical conduct is part of academic integrity because both rest on honesty and responsibility; the form is only the mechanism.

title: Formative check: evaluating against the principles
displayTitle: A study plans to recruit participants by telling them their tutor expects them to take part. Which ESRC principle does this most clearly breach?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Recruiting by saying a tutor expects it breaches which principle?

_items.text: That participation should, wherever possible, be voluntary and appropriately informed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Pressure to take part undermines voluntary participation.

_items.text: That research should maximise benefit and minimise harm.
_items.feedback: That principle is about outcomes, not how people are recruited.

_items.text: That lines of responsibility should be clearly defined.
_items.feedback: Accountability is a separate principle.

_items.text: That the independence of research should be maintained.
_items.feedback: Independence concerns conflicts of interest, not recruitment.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Telling students a tutor expects participation makes it no longer freely voluntary.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which principle is about the freedom to take part?
_incorrect.final: Recruiting through a tutor's expectation breaches voluntary, informed participation; the other principles are about outcomes, accountability and independence.

title: Formative check: anticipating the issues
displayTitle: You are preparing a research-ethics application for a project in {{context}}. Which of these is the ethical issue you most need to anticipate and address?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which ethical issue must a {{context}} application most anticipate?

_items.text: How you will secure voluntary, informed consent and protect participants from harm in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consent and protection from harm are the core ethical issues to address in {{context}}.

_items.text: How quickly you can collect enough data to finish on time.
_items.feedback: That is a project-management concern, not an ethical issue.

_items.text: Which referencing style your {{context}} tutor prefers.
_items.feedback: Referencing style is not an ethics issue.

_items.text: How many sources your {{context}} literature review should contain.
_items.feedback: Source count belongs to writing, not research ethics.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Consent and protection from harm are the ethical issues a {{context}} application must address.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option names an ethical issue rather than a practical or writing one?
_incorrect.final: An ethics application for {{context}} must anticipate how consent is secured and participants protected from harm; the other options are not ethical issues.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Three duties to your participants
body: Handling data responsibly means meeting three duties to the people behind it. Review each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards on the three duties to participants.

_items.title: Confidentiality
_items.subtitle: Protecting the data
_items.text: You have a legal obligation to keep any data not already in the public domain confidential. Store it securely and share it only where you have a clear basis to do so.

_items.title: Informed consent
_items.subtitle: Before you share
_items.text: If you need to share collected data, it is your responsibility to secure participants' consent first, usually through a signed consent form that your university may provide.

_items.title: Anonymisation
_items.subtitle: When you report
_items.text: Where you share data you have consent to use, anonymise responses. Rather than naming a participant, you refer to them as Participant A or Participant B, so individuals cannot be identified.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two researchers finish the same set of participant interviews and turn to writing up.

{{learner-a}} quotes participants by name, emails the raw recordings to a collaborator without asking, and keeps the files on a personal laptop. The write-up reads vividly, but consent was never secured for sharing, and named quotations make individuals identifiable. The duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity have all been missed.

{{learner-b}} secures signed consent before sharing anything, stores the recordings securely, and reports participants as Participant A and Participant B. Where a participant is under eighteen, {{learner-b}} checks the extra requirements with the research ethics committee first. The data still tells its story, but no one can be identified from it.

Both researchers gathered the same material. Only {{learner-b}} treated the people behind the data as owed confidentiality, consent and anonymity.

title: Handling participant data
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Run through these questions whenever you store, share or report data from participants.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Am I keeping all data not in the public domain confidential and secure?
Have I secured participants' consent before sharing any of their data?
Am I using a consent form, whether my university's or one I have prepared?
Have I anonymised responses so individuals cannot be identified?
Where children or vulnerable participants are involved, have I sought the committee's advice?
Do I know who is responsible for the data at each stage?

title: Formative check: duties to participants
displayTitle: A researcher wants to share interview recordings with a collaborator. What must they do first to meet their duties to participants?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What must a researcher do first before sharing recordings?

_items.text: Secure the participants' consent, usually through a signed consent form, before sharing the data.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consent comes before any sharing.

_items.text: Delete the recordings once the collaborator has listened to them.
_items.feedback: Deletion afterwards does not meet the duty to secure consent first.

_items.text: Share the data first and ask the participants afterwards.
_items.feedback: Consent must come before sharing, not after.

_items.text: Publish the recordings so they are in the public domain.
_items.feedback: Publishing identifiable data without consent breaches confidentiality.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Participants' consent must be secured before their data is shared.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What gives you a basis to share the data at all?
_incorrect.final: The first duty is to secure consent, usually in writing, before sharing. The other options share or expose data without that basis.

title: Formative check: vulnerable participants
displayTitle: Why does research involving children or other vulnerable participants call for additional care?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why do children or vulnerable participants need extra care?

_items.text: Because they may be less able to give fully informed, voluntary consent, so extra safeguards and expert advice are needed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reduced capacity to consent calls for further safeguards.

_items.text: Because their data is more interesting to examiners.
_items.feedback: That is not an ethical reason.

_items.text: Because anonymisation is not required for children.
_items.feedback: Anonymisation still applies; the duties tighten, they do not relax.

_items.text: Because consent forms do not apply to anyone under eighteen.
_items.feedback: Consent still applies, with additional safeguards.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reduced capacity to give informed, voluntary consent means extra safeguards and advice are needed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about capacity to consent, not convenience.
_incorrect.final: Children and vulnerable participants may be less able to consent fully, so the duties tighten and expert advice is needed; they do not relax.

title: Formative check: appraising data handling
displayTitle: You have collected participant data for a study in {{context}} and now need to report it. How should you handle that data?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How should participant data in {{context}} be handled?

_items.text: Keep it confidential and secure, share it only with consent, and anonymise responses so participants in {{context}} cannot be identified.
_items.feedback: Yes. Confidentiality, consent and anonymity together protect participants in {{context}}.

_items.text: Name participants in full so the {{context}} findings feel authentic.
_items.feedback: Naming participants breaches anonymity.

_items.text: Email the raw data to anyone in {{context}} who asks for it.
_items.feedback: That breaches confidentiality and consent.

_items.text: Store it on a personal device and share it freely once the project ends.
_items.feedback: Free sharing and insecure storage breach your duties.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Confidentiality, consent and anonymity together protect your {{context}} participants.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option protects participants rather than exposing them?
_incorrect.final: Data in {{context}} must be kept confidential and secure, shared only with consent, and anonymised; the other options expose participants.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Rigour from proposal to dissertation
body: Rigour is sustained across the stages of a project, not clipped on at the end. Reveal each stage to see where integrity is tested.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal where rigour has to hold.

_items.title: Proposal
_items.body: Rigour starts with the proposal. The questions you set, and the methods you choose to answer them, commit you to a design you will have to defend later.

_items.title: Ethical approval
_items.body: Before data collection, your ethics application sets out the research and the issues it raises. Approval is not a hurdle cleared and forgotten; it is a standard you then hold yourself to.

_items.title: Data collection
_items.body: As you gather data, integrity and transparency are tested in practice. You record honestly, keep participants' data secure, and keep clear lines of responsibility for every decision.

_items.title: Analysis
_items.body: In analysis, rigour means letting the evidence speak. You report what you found, including what is inconvenient, and you are clear about what the data will and will not support.

_items.title: Dissertation
_items.body: The dissertation draws all of this together on a grander scale. It is the ultimate test of your research competencies, where the integrity sustained at every earlier stage either holds or shows its gaps.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students reach the final weeks of the same dissertation.

{{learner-a}} treated each stage as a separate box to tick. The proposal promised one method, the data was collected another way, and the ethics approval no longer matches what happened. The write-up is polished, but the gaps between what was proposed, approved and done are visible to any careful reader.

{{learner-b}} kept the thread intact. The questions set in the proposal, the method approved by the ethics committee, and the analysis reported in the dissertation all line up, and every departure is explained with reasons. The work can be defended at each step because its integrity was sustained throughout, not assembled at the end.

Both submitted a dissertation. Only {{learner-b}} could show that rigour held from proposal to submission, which is what the dissertation, as the ultimate test of these competencies, is built to reveal.

title: Sustaining rigour across the project
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Return to these questions at each stage of a project, not only at the end.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Do my research questions, methods and findings still line up with my proposal?
Does what I actually did still match what my ethics approval covered?
Have I explained, with reasons, any departure from the original plan?
Am I reporting the evidence honestly, including what is inconvenient?
Can I say who is accountable for each decision in the project?
Could I defend each stage of this work if a reader questioned it?

title: Formative check: sustaining integrity
displayTitle: What does it mean to sustain research integrity across a whole project?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does sustaining integrity across a project mean?

_items.text: Holding to transparency and clear accountability at every stage, so each decision can be explained and defended.
_items.feedback: Yes. Integrity is sustained through transparency and accountability throughout.

_items.text: Completing the ethics form thoroughly and then not revisiting it.
_items.feedback: Integrity is ongoing, not a one-off form.

_items.text: Producing a long dissertation with many sources.
_items.feedback: Length and source count are not integrity.

_items.text: Keeping the methods secret until the dissertation is submitted.
_items.feedback: Secrecy is the opposite of transparency.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Integrity is sustained by transparency and accountability at every stage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about every stage, not a single step.
_incorrect.final: Sustaining integrity means transparency and accountability throughout, so each decision can be defended; it is not a form, a length or secrecy.

title: Formative check: evaluating rigour
displayTitle: What is the clearest sign that a project has upheld rigour from proposal to dissertation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the clearest sign of rigour across a project?

_items.text: The questions, methods and findings line up across the stages, and any departure from the plan is explained with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Coherence across the stages, with changes explained, is the sign of rigour.

_items.text: The dissertation is longer than the proposal required.
_items.feedback: Length is not rigour.

_items.text: The proposal and the dissertation describe completely different studies.
_items.feedback: That is a loss of the thread, not rigour.

_items.text: No one was able to question the methods used.
_items.feedback: Rigour invites scrutiny rather than avoiding it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Rigour shows as coherence across the stages, with any departure explained.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What links the proposal, the method and the findings?
_incorrect.final: Rigour shows when the questions, methods and findings line up and changes are explained; length, divergence or avoiding scrutiny do not show it.

title: Formative check: defending your decisions
displayTitle: A reader questions whether your {{context}} project was conducted rigorously. Which response best defends your decisions?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How best to defend a {{context}} project's rigour?

_items.text: Showing how your methods followed from your questions, matched your ethics approval, and were applied consistently in {{context}}, with any changes explained.
_items.feedback: Yes. A traceable, transparent account is the strongest defence in {{context}}.

_items.text: Insisting that the dissertation is finished and cannot be revisited.
_items.feedback: That avoids the question.

_items.text: Pointing out that the word count met the {{context}} requirement.
_items.feedback: Word count is not a measure of rigour.

_items.text: Explaining that you ran out of time to follow the original plan.
_items.feedback: Time pressure does not defend a decision on its merits.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A traceable, transparent account of your decisions is the strongest defence in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option accounts for the decisions rather than deflecting?
_incorrect.final: The strongest defence in {{context}} traces methods to questions and approval and explains any change; the others deflect the question.

body: Why is completing a research-ethics application best seen as part of academic integrity?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is a research-ethics application part of academic integrity?

_items.text: Because it requires you to acknowledge and address the ethical issues the principles of sound research raise.
_items.feedback: Yes. The form is where the principles of ethical research are acknowledged and met.

_items.text: Because the university will not mark a dissertation without the form.
_items.feedback: That is a procedural fact, not what makes ethics part of integrity.

_items.text: Because approval proves the findings of the research are correct.
_items.feedback: Approval concerns conduct, not whether findings are correct.

_items.text: Because it is the fastest way to begin collecting data.
_items.feedback: Ethics is about sound conduct, not speed.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The application is where the principles of ethical research are acknowledged and met.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the form asks you to acknowledge.

body: A study describes participation as something a tutor expects of students. Which ESRC principle does this most clearly put at risk?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Describing participation as expected risks which principle?

_items.text: That participation should, wherever possible, be voluntary and appropriately informed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Expected participation is not freely voluntary.

_items.text: That the independence of research should be maintained.
_items.feedback: Independence concerns conflicts of interest, not how participants are recruited.

_items.text: That lines of responsibility should be clearly defined.
_items.feedback: Accountability is a different principle from voluntary participation.

_items.text: That benefit should be maximised and harm minimised.
_items.feedback: That principle is about outcomes, not the freedom to take part.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Participation that is expected rather than freely chosen breaches voluntary, informed participation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which principle is about the freedom to take part?

body: Before sharing collected data with a collaborator, a researcher's first responsibility is to:
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Before sharing data with a collaborator, the first responsibility is to:

_items.text: secure the participants' consent, usually through a signed consent form.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consent must be secured before data is shared.

_items.text: anonymise the collaborator rather than the participants.
_items.feedback: It is the participants whose identities must be protected.

_items.text: publish the data so it enters the public domain.
_items.feedback: Publishing identifiable data without consent breaches confidentiality.

_items.text: delete any data the collaborator does not need.
_items.feedback: Deletion is not what makes sharing permissible; consent is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Sharing data requires participants' consent first, usually in writing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What gives you a basis to share participants' data at all?

body: What is the purpose of referring to people in your data as Participant A and Participant B?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why refer to people as Participant A and Participant B?

_items.text: To anonymise their responses so that individuals cannot be identified.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is anonymisation.

_items.text: To make the dataset look larger than it is.
_items.feedback: Labelling does not change the size of the dataset.

_items.text: To avoid having to secure their consent.
_items.feedback: Anonymising does not remove the need for consent.

_items.text: To speed up the analysis of the results.
_items.feedback: The purpose is protection of identity, not speed.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using labels in place of names anonymises participants' responses.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does replacing names protect?

body: Which of these best shows that rigour has been sustained across a research project?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best shows rigour sustained across a project?

_items.text: The proposal, the approved method and the dissertation line up, and any change is explained with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Coherence across the stages, with changes explained, is the sign of sustained rigour.

_items.text: The dissertation is considerably longer than the proposal.
_items.feedback: Length is not a measure of rigour.

_items.text: The methods were kept confidential until submission.
_items.feedback: Transparency, not secrecy, supports rigour.

_items.text: The project was completed well ahead of the deadline.
_items.feedback: Finishing early says nothing about rigour.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Rigour shows as coherence across the stages, with any departure explained.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What links the proposal, the method and the dissertation?

body: An examiner questions a decision you made during your research. The strongest defence is to:
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: The strongest defence of a research decision is to:

_items.text: show how the decision followed from your questions and your approved method, and account for it transparently.
_items.feedback: Yes. A defensible decision is one you can trace and account for.

_items.text: state that the work is finished and cannot be changed.
_items.feedback: That avoids the question rather than answering it.

_items.text: point out that the dissertation met the word count.
_items.feedback: Word count has no bearing on a decision's soundness.

_items.text: explain that there was not enough time to do otherwise.
_items.feedback: Time pressure does not justify a decision on its merits.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A sound decision is one you can trace to your questions and method and account for openly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What makes a research decision defensible?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: the ethical principles that govern research, the duties you owe the people who provide your data, and the rigour you sustain across a whole project. On their own they can feel like three separate demands. This lesson brings them together into one practice.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not meeting these ideas for the first time. The aim is to stop treating ethics, data and rigour as three separate boxes to tick. Instead you see them as one integrity that runs through every decision you make as a researcher.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together research ethics, responsible data handling and sustained rigour as one research integrity
recognise research integrity at work in a researcher's decisions across a whole project
plan how you will hold your {{context}} research to this one integrity from proposal to dissertation

title: Concept: definition
body: Research integrity is these three strands working as one. Ethical principles tell you how to treat people and why. Responsible data handling is those principles applied to the information participants give you. Sustained rigour is the same integrity held steady across every stage, from proposal to dissertation. They are not three hurdles but one commitment to research that can be trusted and defended.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, research integrity is one thread you carry through a whole project, not three checks you clear and forget. The principles you set at the proposal shape how you treat participants, and how you treat participants shapes what you can honestly report. When the thread holds, your work can be trusted and defended at every stage.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a research project you are planning or undertaking. Where is it most at risk of losing this one integrity, and what is the first thing you would do to protect it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Research integrity is strongest when ethics, data handling and rigour work as one. You carry a single commitment from proposal to dissertation, so that every decision can be trusted and defended. It is the one practice, not any single strand, that makes your research sound.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: Research integrity is one commitment held steadily across every stage of a project. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Set principles
_items.body: At the proposal stage, set out the ethical principles your research must meet.

_items.title: Protect people
_items.body: When you collect data, protect participants through confidentiality, consent and anonymity.

_items.title: Stay aligned
_items.body: As the project runs, keep your methods matching what your ethics approval covered.

_items.title: Show it held
_items.body: In the dissertation, show that this integrity held from proposal to submission.

_diagram.title: Research integrity from proposal to submission

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two researchers finish the same project. One treated ethics, data and rigour as separate jobs: the ethics form was cleared early, the data handled loosely, and the write-up no longer matched the approved plan. The other carried one integrity throughout, so the principles set at the proposal, the care taken with data, and the final dissertation all told one story. Only the second researcher could defend every decision when a reader questioned it.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to keep one integrity across a project
body: Use these questions to check that ethics, data and rigour are working as one across your project.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Do my ethical principles still shape what I actually do, not just the form I filed?
Am I protecting participants' data with the same care I promised at approval?
Do my proposal, my approved method and my findings still line up?
Have I explained, with reasons, any departure from the original plan?
Could I defend each decision to a reader who questioned my research?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat ethics, data handling and rigour as one research integrity rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat ethics, data handling and rigour as one research integrity rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat ethics, data handling and rigour as one research integrity rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because they draw on the same commitment to research people can trust, so a decision in one strand supports the others.
_items.feedback: Yes. One integrity runs through all three, so they hold together.

_items.text: Because treating them separately means you only have to satisfy one of the three.
_items.feedback: All three still matter. Seeing them as one does not let you drop any.

_items.text: Because the ethics form is the only part an examiner ever checks.
_items.feedback: The form is a mechanism, not the point. Integrity is wider than any single check.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than attending to three things.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. Seeing them as one keeps your decisions consistent.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Ethics, data handling and rigour are one commitment to research that can be trusted and defended.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what these three strands have in common.

displayTitle: A researcher sets ethical principles in the proposal, protects participant data as promised, and keeps the method matching approval right through to the dissertation. What does this show?
body: A researcher sets ethical principles in the proposal, protects participant data as promised, and keeps the method matching approval right through to the dissertation. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A researcher sets ethical principles in the proposal, protects participant data as promised, and keeps the method matching approval right through to the dissertation. What does this show?

_items.text: That research integrity is one practice: the same commitment held steady across every stage of the project.
_items.feedback: Yes. Ethics, data and rigour worked as one from start to finish.

_items.text: That the researcher wasted effort by repeating the same check three times.
_items.feedback: These are not repeats. Each strand protects a different part of the same integrity.

_items.text: That only the dissertation stage really matters for integrity.
_items.feedback: Integrity had to hold at every stage, not just the last one.

_items.text: That ethical approval alone guarantees a rigorous project.
_items.feedback: Approval is one step. Rigour is sustained by decisions across the whole project.

_feedback.correct: That's right. One integrity, held across proposal, data and dissertation, is the practice this course builds.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the researcher kept the three strands aligned throughout.

displayTitle: You want to hold your {{context}} research to this one integrity this year. Which plan does that best?
body: You want to hold your {{context}} research to this one integrity this year. Which plan does that best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to hold your your subject research to this one integrity this year. Which plan does that best?

_items.text: Set ethical principles in the proposal, protect {{context}} participants' data as promised, and keep method, approval and write-up aligned.
_items.feedback: Yes. That carries one integrity across your whole {{context}} project.

_items.text: Complete the ethics form quickly, then focus only on getting enough {{context}} data.
_items.feedback: The form is a start, but integrity continues through data and write-up.

_items.text: Keep your {{context}} method to yourself so no one can question it.
_items.feedback: Transparency is part of integrity. Hiding your method weakens it, not protects it.

_items.text: Deal with ethics, data and rigour only if a supervisor asks about them.
_items.feedback: Integrity is something you own across the project, not only when prompted.

_feedback.correct: That's right. One integrity, carried from proposal to dissertation, keeps your {{context}} research trustworthy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps all three strands working together.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to treat research integrity as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: What does it mean to treat research integrity as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to treat research integrity as one practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Holding ethics, responsible data handling and rigour together as one commitment across the whole project.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands are one integrity.

_items.text: Completing the ethics form and then not thinking about integrity again.
_items.feedback: The form is one step; integrity continues through the project.

_items.text: Focusing on whichever strand an examiner is most likely to check.
_items.feedback: All three matter together, whoever is checking.

_items.text: Keeping ethics, data and rigour in separate stages that never connect.
_items.feedback: They connect, and that connection is the integrity.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student's proposal, approved method and dissertation tell one coherent story, and their participants' data was protected throughout. What does this best show?
body: A student's proposal, approved method and dissertation tell one coherent story, and their participants' data was protected throughout. What does this best show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student's proposal, approved method and dissertation tell one coherent story, and their participants' data was protected throughout. What does this best show?

_items.text: That research integrity was sustained as one practice from proposal to submission.
_items.feedback: Yes. One integrity held across every stage.

_items.text: That the dissertation was simply longer than the proposal required.
_items.feedback: Length is not integrity. The alignment across stages is.

_items.text: That ethical approval on its own made the project rigorous.
_items.feedback: Approval is one step; rigour is sustained by decisions throughout.

_items.text: That the student can ignore data duties once the write-up begins.
_items.feedback: Data duties hold throughout, including at write-up.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
